Few statistics ignite faster partisan headlines than claiming a county carries "more registered voters than living adult citizens." Yet dividing an exact county registration count on a Tuesday morning by a multi-year Census survey sample without incorporating confidence intervals and migration lag guarantees false positives. Applied [mathematics](/explore/mathematics) requires treating the denominator as an interval estimate rather than an exact headcount.

The Census Bureau states plainly why its Citizen Voting Age Population (CVAP) special tabulation behaves differently from decennial headcounts:

> "The 2020-2024 CVAP tables pool sixty monthly American Community Survey interviews collected across five years, yielding a period estimate bounded by a published 90 percent margin of error."

Two statistical properties follow directly from pooling five years of household surveys across 240,833,718 estimated U.S. citizen adults in the 2020-2024 file. First, rural counties with only a few thousand residents exhibit proportionally larger confidence margins because fewer households enter each five-year sample. Second, a five-year average centered near mid-2022 structurally understates rapid post-2022 population inflows and overstates sudden outflows. Even without administrative error, a boomtown county adding thousands of new retirees per year can cross 100% of a five-year moving average simply because DMV voter applications update daily while ACS five-year pooled surveys crawl forward one fifth per year.

## Applying the Upper 90% MOE Bound in North Carolina and Mississippi

Testing `active_voters > (cvap_2024 + cvap_moe_90)` filters out statistical noise immediately when auditing state registration files against [Marigold Insights](/explore/marigoldinsights) datasets built inside browser [databases](/explore/databases): 1. **Growth-Induced Exceedance in North Carolina:** Across all 100 North Carolina counties (7,898,142 CVAP vs. 6,902,431 active voters and 7,900,954 total registered), only one county crosses the upper 90% bound: Brunswick County reports 136,822 active voters against 128,976 ± 410 CVAP (106.08%). Crucially, Census Population Estimates show Brunswick absorbed +33,821 net domestic in-migrants between 2020 and 2024—an influx of new coastal residents who register immediately upon moving while five-year pooled ACS averages catch up slowly. 2. **Out-Migration Lag in Mississippi:** Across 82 Mississippi counties (2,221,778 CVAP vs.

1,882,342 active voters and 2,112,449 total registered), seven counties surpass the upper 90% CVAP bound—including Humphreys (6,404 active vs. 5,520 ± 23 CVAP, or 116.01%), Tallahatchie (103.94%), Smith (101.93%), Yazoo (101.88%, -3,507 net domestic migration), Hancock (101.81%, +1,114 migration), Holmes (101.25%), and Hinds (165,189 active vs. 164,779 ± 368 CVAP, 100.25%, amid -17,670 net domestic out-migration). Here, sustained departures outpace two-cycle statutory inactive purges, elevating ratios in the opposite demographic direction from Brunswick.

## Building an Honest Triage Score Without False Alarms

Evaluating both states side by side clarifies why single-column red flags fail public discourse. An effective audit rule weights active registration against `cvap_upper_bound_90` first, then inspects `net_domestic_mig_2020_2024`, `deaths_2020_2024`, and Section 8 `A10a` confirmation notice velocity. Counties crossing `100%` via booming inward migration require updated polling precinct staffing and extra ballot printers; counties crossing `100%` amid steep out-migration need targeted address confirmation mailings.

## The Honest Counterargument: Does Adding 90% MOE Hide Genuine Over-Registration?

Critics of wide confidence thresholds worry that allowing active rolls to exceed central CVAP estimates until clearing `cvap_2024 + cvap_moe_90` creates a blind spot in mid-sized counties where a 3% administrative over-count falls inside normal sampling noise. Conversely, even `cvap_upper_bound_90` leaves real structural lags visible only when counties cross 100% rather than flagging whether 98% represents sluggish NVRA list maintenance in a low-turnout county.

The disciplined solution uses CVAP margins as a triage ranker rather than a courtroom verdict. Pairing upper-bound exceedance tests with raw `active_to_cvap_pct`, cumulative 2020-2024 deaths, `A10a` confirmation mailings, and domestic migration separates growth booms from dormant rural rolls cleanly—ensuring [election integrity](/explore/election-integrity) oversight focuses on operational capacity instead of statistical artifacts.

---
**Sources:** [U.S. Census 2020-2024 CVAP Special Tabulation](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/decennial/rdo/datasets/2024/2024-cvap/CVAP_2020-2024_ACS_csv_files.zip) · [U.S. Census ACS Design & Methodology](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/methodology/design-and-methodology.html) · [U.S. Census 2020-2024 County Population Components](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/datasets/2020-2024/counties/totals/co-est2024-alldata.csv)

Public debates over election operations routinely treat ballot delivery and poll-book accuracy as separate worlds. Federal county totals from the 2024 EAVS V2.0 release demonstrate why both functions act as connected pressure gauges on the exact same address database. When counties fail to track residential moves cleanly across Sections A, C, and E, undeliverable mail packets spike weeks before Election Day and provisional ballot lines lengthen on Election Night.

Election administrators measure mail-delivery friction explicitly across EAVS Section C fields tracking packets leaving county vaults versus packets bouncing back undelivered. As EAC survey instructions note:

> "Jurisdictions report total domestic and UOCAVA mail ballots transmitted (`C1a`) alongside ballots returned as undeliverable (`C1c`) and total provisional ballots cast (`E1a`) and rejected (`E1d`)."

Across matched U.S. counties inside the 2024 benchmark atlas, local officials transmitted 66,149,059 mail ballots (`C1a`) and logged 915,949 packets returned undeliverable (`C1c`)—an aggregate 1.38% postal bounce rate across hundreds of millions of citizens, accompanied by 1,690,565 provisional ballots cast (`E1a`) and 422,940 provisional ballots rejected (`E1d`), or 25.02% of provisional casts failing statutory verification. Paired inside [Marigold Insights](/explore/marigoldinsights) SQL templates, those four fields surface operational bottlenecks before primary season begins.

## Why Undeliverable Mail and Provisional Rates Move Together

Inspecting county outcomes across [election integrity](/explore/election-integrity) distributions exposes three operational friction points linking Sections A, C, and E:

1. **Stale Mailing Addresses Feed Postal Bounces:** Counties holding high shares of unconfirmed inactive voters or uncollected residential moves automatically mail ballots to outdated apartments when permanent mail-list or universal mail delivery triggers. Tracking `eavs_mail_undeliverable / NULLIF(eavs_mail_transmitted, 0)` pinpoints specific metro counties where apartment turnover outstrips NCOA Postal Service updates. 2. **Provisional Rejection Follows Unreconciled Roll Transitions:** When voters arrive at precincts believing they remain registered after a recent cross-county move or unreturned mail-ballot request, precinct judges issue provisional paper ballots.

Across states without same-day registration or cross-county transfer cures, up to a quarter or more of those provisional casts—part of 422,940 rejections nationwide—are subsequently discarded for out-of-jurisdiction assignment or unregistered status. 3. **Administrative Early-Warning Signals:** High mail-undeliverable counts do not only represent wasted postage and paper stock; returned packets immediately trigger statutory NVRA Section 8 confirmation notice mailings (`A10a`), starting the legal clock that turns uncollected mail errors into future roll removals (`A12a`). Tracking `C1c` thus previews where roll churn will concentrate in the following federal cycle.

## Designing Better Precinct Workflows Around Section E Telemetry

Rather than treating high provisional rejection totals strictly as partisan disputes, [systems design](/explore/systems-design) teams inside state election offices can map high-rejection precincts directly against multi-unit apartment turnover and university zip codes. Deploying dedicated regional lookup tablets, clearer out-of-precinct directional signage, and automated SMS cure portals turns frustrating provisional rejections into verified ballots before county canvasses close.

## The Counterargument: Why High Provisional Volumes Can Reflect Safeguards, Not Failure

County directors in states offering broad provisional cures or disaster-displaced voting emphasize an essential caveat: elevated provisional ballot counts (`E1a`) do not automatically signify polling-place breakdown. During storms or sudden [disaster continuity](/explore/disaster-continuity) emergency relocations, provisional ballots serve precisely as an explicit failsafe ensuring every displaced citizen leaves a reviewable paper record even when precinct computers lose connectivity or voters present outside their assigned precinct.

Separating provisional *casts* from provisional *rejections* resolves that ambiguity analytically. When SQL queries flag high mail-undeliverable rates alongside high *rejection* ratios specifically during quiet weather cycles, counties earn clear targets for USPS National Change of Address syncing and clearer voter-portal status alerts—lowering administrative friction long before ballots enter the mail stream.

---
**Sources:** [U.S. EAC 2024 EAVS V2.0 Public Release](https://www.eac.gov/sites/default/files/2026-02/2024_EAVS_for_Public_Release_nolabel_V2_csv.zip) · [MIT Election Data Lab Mail Voting Research](https://electionlab.mit.edu/research/voting-mail-and-absentee-voting) · [USPS Election Mail Resources](https://about.usps.com/what/government-services/election-mail/)

Conversations around voter-roll accuracy often get trapped inside single-cycle snapshots while overlooking the single largest driver of statutory list attrition: human mortality and residential relocation across four-year presidential cycles. Joining four years of Census county vital statistics directly to federal removal totals provides an objective demographic yardstick that no partisan talking point can distort.

Federal population accounting highlights the baseline turnover every election clerk must process simply to hold rolls steady. As Census county population component methodologies describe:

> "Annual county population estimates track cumulative natural change through vital registration births and `DEATHS` counts paired with IRS and Medicare-derived domestic migration series from April 2020 onward."

Across matched U.S. counties from 2020 through 2024, Census estimates record 13,988,011 cumulative resident deaths (`DEATHS2020`–`DEATHS2024`). Meanwhile, matched county reporting in the 2024 EAVS cycle reflects 20,021,606 total voter removals (`A12a`) alongside 35,328,942 confirmation notices (`A10a`), while certified general-election presidential votes stood at 154,277,745 in 2024 compared with 156,217,931 in 2020.

## Testing Mecklenburg, Wake, and Rural County Attrition

Putting deaths, removals, and certified votes into one [local-first](/explore/local-first) table lets analysts benchmark whether a county's removal engine keeps pace with basic vital records and household churn: 1.

**Urban Churn Balance in North Carolina:** Mecklenburg County, North Carolina recorded 31,883 resident deaths across 2020-2024 alongside 122,082 total voter removals and 88,480 confirmation notices during the 2024 EAVS cycle—demonstrating steady statutory list hygiene through both vital-record matches and interstate address notifications, even as certified presidential ballots climbed from 567,053 in 2020 to 573,679 in 2024. Wake County paired 104,164 removals with 56,879 notices, while Guilford logged 50,218 removals across the same cycle. 2. **Statewide Removals vs. Vital Baseline:** Across North Carolina as a whole, 971,554 removals in 2024 reflect continuous state-to-county vital statistics integration and active Section 8 mailing queues.

Across Mississippi's 82 counties, 148,200 removals paired with 100,185 notices produced a noticeably slower attrition curve relative to population turnover. When any county exhibits total two-year removals markedly below half of four-year adult mortality without compensatory confirmation mailings, auditors immediately identify stalled vital-statistics file transfers between health departments and county clerks. 3. **Validating Certified Returns Against Roll Totals:** Joining certified county returns (`154.27M` national in 2024) against active registrations (`203.68M` active) inside [Marigold Insights](/explore/marigoldinsights) SQL views checks turnout ratios cleanly—highlighting jurisdictions where absentee surges, rapid suburban growth, or post-storm turnout drops explain ballot volume shifts transparently.

## The Honest Counterargument on Raw Death-to-Removal Ratios

Demographic analysts warn against expecting a mechanical one-to-one ratio between Census county `DEATHS` and EAVS voter removals. First, Census death figures include minors, non-citizens, and unregistered adults—populations never present on voter rolls in the first place. Second, multi-year EAVS cycles record removals from two years rather than the full 2020-2024 window, while counties also remove relocating residents alongside deceased registrants. Third, states allocate vital-statistics matching across different statutory windows—some process death certificates weekly through automated Secretary of State interfaces, while others rely on monthly county coroner or health department batch transfers that clump removals irregularly across quarterly reports.

Respecting those nuances keeps [election integrity](/explore/election-integrity) benchmarking grounded in [mathematics](/explore/mathematics). Rather than asserting every resident death must map cleanly to a voter deletion, auditors use Census mortality and domestic out-migration strictly as lower-bound sanity checks: flagging outlier counties whose vital-statistics interfaces or confirmation mailings stall altogether, long before unmaintained rolls turn into administrative headlines or trigger contentious pre-election emergency purges under federal Section 8 deadlines.

When county boards pair annual `DEATHS` mortality benchmarks with automated state-agency records inside open DuckDB tables, bipartisan observers gain a quiet, verifiable baseline that separates natural demographic turnover from operational neglect without exposing individual deceased voters' identities.

---
**Sources:** [tonmcg / MEDSL County Presidential Returns 2024 CSV](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tonmcg/US_County_Level_Election_Results_08-24/master/2024_US_County_Level_Presidential_Results.csv) · [U.S. Census County Population Estimates All-Data 2020-2024](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/datasets/2020-2024/counties/totals/co-est2024-alldata.csv) · [U.S. EAC 2024 EAVS V2.0 CSV Release](https://www.eac.gov/sites/default/files/2026-02/2024_EAVS_for_Public_Release_nolabel_V2_csv.zip)

Thousands of civic researchers download the federal Election Assistance Commission's EAVS spreadsheet each cycle, run a quick spreadsheet sum across a registration or mail-ballot column, and publish wildly distorted national totals without realizing the file contains negative error sentinels, mixed municipal-and-county reporting grains, and variable renumbering between election cycles. Understanding those structural traps transforms raw federal CSV drops into dependable [databases](/explore/databases) tables.

Federal survey methodologists encode missingness explicitly inside numerical variables rather than leaving blank strings everywhere. As the 2024 EAVS documentation explains:

> "Negative response codes such as -77, -88, and -99 distinguish valid survey skips, not-applicable statutory procedures, and unreported county values from genuine zero observations."

Treating `-88` as zero or leaving `-99` in a column sum skews state comparisons instantly. Filtering negative sentinels before arithmetic is step one in any reproducible workflow highlighted across [Marigold Insights](/explore/marigoldinsights). In the Feb 2026 V2.0 file containing 6,461 raw local jurisdictions, summing cleaned positive Section A metrics yields 38,803,086 confirmation notices and 21,298,175 total voter removals nationwide before pruning non-state territories down to the 3,222-county U.S. atlas covering 226,420,603 registered voters.

## Three Schema Gotchas in the 2024 V2.0 Release

Analysts porting queries written against earlier 2020 EAVS schemas regularly break silently unless they inspect three structural shifts documented directly in the Feb 2026 headers:

1. **Section A Variable Renumbering:** Do not reuse 2020 EAVS column names blindly. In 2024 V2.0, `A10a` records total confirmation notices sent under NVRA Section 8 (35,328,942 across 50 states + DC matched), while `A12a` captures total voters removed from registration rolls (20,021,606 matched). Meanwhile `A1a`, `A1b`, and `A1c` continue separating total registered (226,420,603), active (203,680,591), and inactive (22,588,570) baselines. Similarly, mail ballot outreach and rejections live in `C1a` (66,149,059 transmitted) and `C1c` (915,949 undeliverable), while provisional outcomes track cleanly in `E1a` (1,690,565 cast) and `E1d` (422,940 rejected). 2. **California Nine-Digit Leading-Zero Stripping:** Spreadsheet tools and naive CSV parsers frequently drop leading zeros from California FIPS identifiers like `0600100000`, producing 9-digit strings (`600100000`).

Left-padding numerical codes under ten digits back to ten characters recovers accurate 5-digit county slicing across all 58 California counties instead of misaligning Alameda and Los Angeles rows. 3. **Sub-County Grain in New England and Wisconsin:** Maine, Massachusetts, Connecticut, Vermont, and Wisconsin report EAVS operations at town or municipal level (`3,334` sub-county units inside 2024 EAVS). Joining them unaggregated against county-level Census tables fails unless municipal FIPS rows map upward to parent county FIPS codes—using Wisconsin's `Jurisdiction_Name` suffix convention and state town-to-county lookups to collapse 6,461 raw rows smoothly into 3,127 five-digit EAVS counties.

## Reproducible SQL Cleaning Pattern for Browser Engines

When analysts ingest raw municipal CSVs inside WebAssembly SQL pipelines, asserting sentinel hygiene in a single `NULLIF` or `CASE WHEN col >= 0 THEN col ELSE 0 END` pass prevents silent arithmetic drift. Validating row counts before and after aggregation catches accidental duplicate joins immediately—confirming that 3,222 county atlas keys match exact one-to-one state totals reported in official certifications.

## The Counterargument: Does County Rollup Hide Town-Level Disparity?

Local clerks in New England town-meeting states raise an authentic methodological concern: rolling dozens of towns into a single Massachusetts or Connecticut county average masks whether a specific urban town hall suffered unusually high provisional ballot rejections or mail undeliverables compared with neighboring suburbs.

That observation illustrates why clean data architecture stores both the raw 6,461-row FIPS grain internally and the normalized 3,127-county crosswalk externally. By keeping sub-county aggregation rules transparent and inspectable inside [systems design](/explore/systems-design) pipelines, researchers gain apple-to-apple national joins against Census CVAP and MEDSL returns while remaining free to drill back into individual town IDs whenever town-level [election integrity](/explore/election-integrity) questions arise.

---
**Sources:** [U.S. EAC 2024 EAVS V2.0 CSV Release](https://www.eac.gov/sites/default/files/2026-02/2024_EAVS_for_Public_Release_nolabel_V2_csv.zip) · [U.S. Census ANSI & FIPS County Reference](https://www.census.gov/library/reference/code-lists/ansi.html) · [MIT Election Data and Science Lab Methodology](https://electionlab.mit.edu/research)
